spots.name: The Venetian Macao
spots.label: Venetian Macao

text.geographic_location: On the Cotai Strip, built on reclaimed land, in the Cotai area of Macau, among a group of large resorts.
text.access_note: The resort is a commercial complex with shops, a casino and an arena, so check the official site before you go for any access rules.
text.directions_text: Head for the Cotai Strip resort area and look for The Venetian Macao. The resort also runs its own private buses, and Cotai West station on the Macau LRT is within reach. Once inside, make your way to the 2nd floor and look for Lord Stow's Bakery; the small bridge is beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description: The Venetian Macao is a huge hotel and casino resort on the Cotai Strip, modelled on its sister resort in Las Vegas. The main tower has 39 storeys and the resort opened on 28 August 2007. Inside there are around 300 shops and an indoor canal, which is what makes it so photogenic: the corridors look like a Venetian street, with a painted sky overhead. This spot's photo is taken indoors, from the small bridge on the 2nd floor beside Lord Stow's Bakery. Look diagonally down the corridor and you get a long, nearly empty view with the painted-sky light falling through the space. One guide suggests it as a quieter alternative to the busy bridge over the Grand Canal. The resort is very large, so allow time to find your way inside. The exterior of the building doesn't appear in this view. If you want the canal, Grand Canal Shoppes shows a gondola under the painted sky with the Venetian-style facades behind it. For a night-time frame of the lit frontage and the red buses, try Starlight Bridge. For the corridor shot, stand still, keep the phone level and let the perspective do the work. Shoot a few frames with and without people walking through, then pick the cleanest.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the corridor. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the ceiling and the full sweep of the space, but keep the phone level so the lines don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright painted sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the ceiling isn't washed out. Hold the phone steady with both hands; if night mode switches on in dim areas, stay still until it finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (small bridge on the 2nd floor beside the bakery; shoot diagonally down the corridor). A diagonal view down a nearly empty interior corridor, with the fake-sky light falling through the space. From here the photo shows a diagonal view down a nearly empty interior corridor, with the fake-sky light falling through the space.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 4 PM, when sunlight shines through the painted sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Aim diagonally down the corridor rather than straight along it, so the lines lead the eye into the picture. Switch on gridlines and use them to keep the verticals straight. If you also want the canal, Grand Canal Shoppes is the alternative viewpoint, with a gondola under the painted sky.

text.geographic_location: The Grand Lisboa is in Sé, on the Macau Peninsula.
text.access_note: Rua Nova à Guia is an ordinary public street with no entry fee, but it is busy with traffic. For the hotel and casino themselves, check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops listed nearby, so make your way to the Grand Lisboa in Sé on foot or by a ride of your choice, or to the Mei Ka Building, which some guides use as the navigation target for the street. From the Grand Lisboa, head north-east to Rua Nova à Guia, about 430 m on foot. Walk on the left-hand pavement and look back towards the south-west to see the tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description:
The Grand Lisboa is a 47-floor, 261-metre hotel tower in Sé, and it is the tallest building in Macau. Its casino and restaurants opened in February 2007 and the hotel followed in December 2008. It was designed by the Hong Kong architects Dennis Lau and Ng Chun Man. It is the most distinctive part of Macau's skyline.

The best-known phone photo is taken from Rua Nova à Guia. From the left-hand pavement, the tower rises above low, older residential buildings along the street. That mix of old and new is what makes this the classic postcard view of the hotel. Several guides call it the signature Grand Lisboa shot, and one says the left side of the road gives the best angle.

The street is residential and the traffic is heavy, so stay on the pavement and never step into the road to line up a shot. Start with the default lens (1x) and let the street lead the eye towards the tower. If the top is cut off, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) or step back along the pavement. Early morning is quieter and the sun is less harsh, though another guide finds the afternoon light kinder.

If you want a different view, Guia Hill Municipal Park gives an elevated panorama over the peninsula. Nam Van Lake shows the tower across the water, often with city lights reflected in it.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the top of the tower is cut off, or the telephoto (2x or more) to bring the tower closer above the older buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Wipe the lens first, then take a few frames between passing vehicles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rua Nova à Guia (left-hand sidewalk, with the hotel behind you; one guide says Mei Ka Building is the navigation target). The Grand Lisboa tower rises above low, older residential buildings along the street, creating the old-versus-new contrast that makes this the classic postcard frame. From here the Grand Lisboa lies to the south-west, rising above the low residential buildings along the street. Keep to the pavement because the traffic is heavy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is quieter for traffic and the sun is gentler. One guide finds the afternoon light favourable, so you could try both.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines. Let the street and the older buildings fill the lower part of the frame, so the old-versus-new contrast is clear. If you want another angle, Guia Hill Municipal Park or Nam Van Lake also show the tower.

spots.name: Macau Tower
spots.label: Macau Tower

text.geographic_location: Macau Tower is in the Sé area of the Macau peninsula, on reclaimed land in the Nam Van area. The lakeside promenade where you take the photo is a short walk to the north-east, facing the tower across the water.
text.access_note: The lakeside promenade is a free, open public space; the tower's observation deck and activities are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Head for the Nam Van area on the southern side of the Macau peninsula and use a map app to reach Nam Van Lake or Macau Tower. Walk along the lakeside promenade with the tower behind you, then turn round to take the photo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description:
Macau Tower is the tall, slim tower on the southern side of the Macau peninsula. It stands 338 m high and is used for viewing, entertainment, telecommunications and broadcasting. It was opened on 19 December 2001 and was inspired by the Sky Tower in Auckland, New Zealand. It sits on land created by the Nam Van reclamation project, which added 130 hectares and made the peninsula about 20% bigger.

It photographs well because its shape is simple and clear against the sky, and the open water in front of it gives you room to step back and fit it all in. The best-known place to shoot it is the lakeside promenade at Nam Van Lake. The tower rises above the lake and the waterfront skyline, and on calm evenings the lights are often reflected in the water. As you walk along the promenade the tower stays in view, so you can try several angles before choosing one.

For a phone, turn the phone upright (portrait) so the full height fits, and keep some water in the bottom of the frame for the reflection. Wait for a moment when the surface is still. If you want a different view, Sai Van Bridge shows the tower framed by its reflection in the still lake water beside the bridge, and the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha gives a wider view across the hill and lakes with the tower in the distance. The promenade is the easiest option.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see the tower with the lake and skyline around it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more water and reflection, or to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tower's shape against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or hold your breath as you shoot to avoid blur. Tap the tower to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down so the tower lights do not blow out.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Nam Van Lake (lakeside promenade facing the tower). The tower rising above the lake and the waterfront skyline, often with reflections in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or after dark, when the tower and skyline lights are on and the reflections are strongest.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on gridlines so the tower stands straight against a vertical line. Leave a band of water along the bottom to catch the reflection. If you have time, Sai Van Bridge or the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha give different views of the tower.
